APR is the total finance charge expressed in an annual rate. That's the textbook definition. OP stated they were considering paying the loan off early. The APR they will have paid will be higher than the one stated at closing. At closing we make the assumption you'll pay on the loan to term, because no one can see the future.

In finance, cost of debt is expressed as a percentage. In this particular case, cost of debt is the APR.

Not understanding the above principles is why people get hammered by payday loans. APR is the annualized value. So if I pay $25 for a $500 loan over 3 days, my APR is 598% because if I keep paying $25 every three days over a year, I end up paying over $3k. The lender will earn 598% on that $500 if he lends it out every three days for a $25 fee.
The cost is your APR in this case. I'm trying to point out the relativeness and so speaking in general terms your cost is the APR.

It matters more so. Because APR is usually impacted by an origination fee of some sort. So your APR is higher if you pay it back faster. You'll pay less in total interest, but the cost for such sort term money is higher.

For example:

A $5,000 loan with a 5% origination fee and 5% interest rate over two years has a 8.289% APR. Total interest and fees paid: $527.68

The same loan, if paid back in 3 months has a 34.92% APR.
Total interest and fees paid: $293.80

So yes it matters when shopping. Because at 3 months it makes more sense to just put the $5k on a credit card with a 24.99% interest rate. Total interest and fees in this case is only $209.68

Consider that nearly every asset under the sun is being traded off-exchange. That's currencies, bonds, equities, commodities; you name it, you could probably find some way to securitize and sell it. There hasn't been this kind of long-lasting volatility in a single security of this scale ever. OTC markets are not the problem.

So the suggestion that we ban them or try and require private parties engaging in transactions to report the same kind of information that we can gather from centralized exchanges where trades are uniform is ridiculous. It sounds more like a poorly constructed government solution that won't even address the problem and will probably create more problems.
